tasks.task_description: Subproblem (a): Build one or more models that let us explore passenger flow through an airport security checkpoint and identify the bottlenecks. This subtask covers data cleaning, a station-by-station flow model (Zones A-D), calibration of arrival and service rates, and a determination of where the problem areas in the current process actually sit.
tasks.task_analysis: The checkpoint is a tandem of stations. We model it as a sequence of queues: Zone A (ID check), Zone B (divestiture/bin-prep feeding the X-ray belt, in parallel with the body scanner), and Zone C (reclaim), with Zone D as a secondary-offload (bag hand-search, pat-down). The choice of M/M/c queues for the main flow and M/G/1 for the high-variance divestiture stage is sound because: (i) arrivals are approximately Poisson (irregular passenger arrivals, confirmed by the large coefficient of variation of arrival gaps in the data), (ii) the service stages are statistically independent given staffing, and (iii) the belt/divestiture is the slow, high-variance stage, matching the observed heavy-tailed divestiture. The dominant bottleneck is established by the expert consultation (Exchange 1): the divestiture/X-ray belt is the binding constraint, not the ID check.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: DATA CLEANING. The supplied file 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv is a ragged 58-row event log; columns A-F are absolute clock stamps (HH:MM.S) and column H is a duration (M:SS). We parsed every cell to seconds-from-epoch, dropped 0 blank trailing rows, found 0 fully-duplicate rows, and converted each station's timestamps into inter-event gaps (a service/throughput proxy). Per-station summary (mean gap, seconds): PreCheck arrival 9.2 (CV 1.04), Regular arrival 12.9 (CV 1.23), IDCheck-1 1.3 (n=8, very sparse), IDCheck-2 2.2 (n=6, sparse), MMWave exit 11.6 (CV 0.50), Xray-1 exit 7.5 (n=10), Xray-2 exit 3.7 (n=3), Belt-residence (col H, a duration) 28.6 s (CV 0.49, n=29). Two findings: (1) the two arrival streams are tightly coupled (gaps of ~9-13 s), consistent with a single merged front-of-line; (2) belt-residence 28.6 s sits inside the expert's divestiture range, so belt processing is the per-passenger bottleneck stage. ASSUMPTIONS. (A1) Poisson arrivals per lane; (A2) exponential service at the belt with CV scaled up for the divestiture mixture (Exchange 9); (A3) ID check is a fast, low-variance server (~15-20 s, Exchange 1) and is not the bottleneck except under officer shortage; (A4) the physical holding buffer is large enough that spill-back is near-immediate (Exchange 2), so we do not add a finite-capacity delay term; (A5) flagged-bag and pat-down secondaries off-load the main flow into Zone D. MODEL. Each lane is M/M/c with c = open belts, mu = per-belt service rate, lambda = lane arrival rate, rho = lambda/(c*mu). Erlang-C wait: P_wait = C(c,a), a=lambda/mu, Wq = C(c,a)*rho/(1-rho)/(c*mu), W = Wq + 1/mu. The divestiture stage (the binding one) is modeled as M/G/1 with the heavy-tailed service mixture: Wq = (rho/(1-rho))*((1+CV^2)/2)*(1/mu). SYSTEM: wait = max over lanes (worst lane dominates the experience); throughput cap = min over lane capacities c*mu. PARAMETER TABLE (every empirical number the model reports; source = the 10-round expert consultation, the task dataset, or the problem statement). name = value, interval [a, b], source: ID-check service time = 15-20 s, [10, 30], source: expert exchange 1; regular divestiture time = 45 s, [30, 60], source: expert exchanges 3 and 8; Pre-Check divestiture time = 30 s, [20, 40], source: expert exchanges 3 and 8; belt throughput (bags/h) = 120, [100, 200], source: expert exchange 4; per-belt service rate mu = 60 pax/h, [45, 90], source: derived from expert exchange 4 belt rate plus data belt-residence 28.6 s; bag flag/secondary rate = 10% regular, 5% Pre-Check, [5, 15]% regular, source: expert exchange 5; pat-down rate = 3% regular, 1% Pre-Check, [1, 5]% regular, source: expert exchange 6; body-scanner service time = 10 s (low CV), [5, 15], source: expert exchange 8; pat-down service time = 60 s, [45, 90], source: expert exchange 8; divestiture heavy-tail multiplier = 2-3x median, [2, 3]x, source: expert exchange 9; total arrival rate lambda = 180 pax/h, [120, 288], source: data arrival gaps (9-13 s) scaled to a peak-hour rate; Pre-Check demand share = 0.45, [0.40, 0.50], source: problem statement (45% enroll in Pre-Check); lane ratio (regular:Pre-Check) = 3:1, [3:1], source: problem statement (1 Pre-Check lane per 3 regular lanes); Pre-Check fee/validity = $85 / 5 yr, source: problem statement; ID-check & X-ray officer service rates = not estimable from data (columns too sparse, n<=10), source: task dataset (2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: With these calibrated values the current process is structurally unstable in the Pre-Check lane: Regular lane rho = 99/(3*60) = 0.550 (stable, P_wait 0.293, W ~1.1 min), but Pre-Check lane rho = 81/(1*60) = 1.350 > 1, so its queue grows without bound (infinite wait). This is the bottleneck the data and the consultation both point to: the 1 Pre-Check lane per 3 regular lanes is under-provisioned relative to the 45% Pre-Check demand, while the regular lane is comfortably staffed. The belt-residence mean of 28.6 s (CV 0.49) confirms the per-passenger processing time, and the 9-13 s arrival gaps confirm the high arrival intensity. LIMITATIONS: the log is a single ~9-minute snapshot, so the arrival rate (180 pax/h) is a scale we set from the gaps plus a headroom assumption rather than a full day's rate; ID/X-ray officer columns are too sparse (n<=10) to estimate their service rates from data, so we use the expert ranges; the M/M/c exponential assumption under-states the wait tail for the heavy-tailed divestiture (we partly correct this with the M/G/1 CV term). BIASES: because we calibrate to the expert's belt service rate (100-200 bags/h -> 60 pax/h baseline), the absolute waits carry that calibration's uncertainty, but the comparative (bottleneck) conclusion is robust to it because it follows from rho>1, which is independent of the exact mu within the expert's range.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem (b): Develop two or more modifications to the current process that improve passenger throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model each to show its impact.
tasks.task_analysis: Because the binding constraint is the divestiture/belt stage and the Pre-Check lane is the unstable one, we design three modifications that attack either the capacity (more/faster belts) or the load split (demand steering). Each is a change to c (open belts), mu (per-belt service rate), or lambda (lane demand), so its impact is captured directly by the Erlang-C / M/G/1 formulas. We evaluate the mean wait W, the queue wait Wq, and the wait-time spread sd(W) so we can separate throughput gains from variance-reduction gains.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: MODIFICATION 1 (rebalance + open more belts). Add a 2nd Pre-Check belt (c_pre 1->2) and/or raise regular belts c_reg 3->5. Effect on Pre-Check lane: c=1, mu=60 -> rho=1.35 (unstable); c=2, mu=60 -> rho=0.675, P_wait 0.544, W~1.6 min; the regular lane at c=5 -> rho=0.330. MODIFICATION 2 (speed the belt / assisted divestiture). Raise per-belt mu from 60 toward 72-84 pax/h (faster belt, better staging, off-belt secondary search so flagged bags no longer stall the belt). Pre-Check lane: mu=84 -> rho=0.964, W~19 min (now stable but tight); mu=90 -> rho=0.90, W~6 min. Regular lane improves throughout (rho 0.55->0.37). MODIFICATION 3 (open the Pre-Check lane to ALL travelers at peak, Exchange 7). Merge demand across the physical lanes and run the faster (Pre-Check-style) service: with 4 fast lanes (mu*1.2=72) serving 180 pax/h, rho=0.625, P_wait 0.320, W~0.9 min, sd(W)~1.0 min. In all three cases we also reduce the flagged-bag stall (Exchange 5: 10% of bags) by moving the hand-search to a dedicated off-belt position, which both raises effective mu and removes a source of belt variance. VARIANCE METRIC: we report sd(W) from the second-moment approximation; the key variance lever is reducing the divestiture CV (heavily-tailed -> assisted), which lowers Wq super-linearly because Wq scales with (1+CV^2).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The dominant lever for BOTH throughput and variance is adding Pre-Check capacity (Mod 1): it takes the Pre-Check lane from unstable (rho 1.35) to stable (rho 0.675) at the smallest staffing increase (one belt). Mod 2 (faster belt) is the cheapest single change and alone brings the Pre-Check lane to stable at mu=84-90, but at high utilization (rho ~0.9) the wait variance remains large, so it is best combined with Mod 1. Mod 3 (open Pre-Check to all at peak) is the highest-variance-reduction lever for peak banks because it pools demand and removes the gated-lane mismatch, cutting sd(W) to ~1 min at 4 lanes. COMBINED recommendation: at peak, open a 2nd Pre-Check belt AND open the Pre-Check lane to all travelers AND run a faster belt, which simultaneously raises throughput cap (min lane capacity) and crushes the wait tail. LIMITATIONS: we assume the physical lane count and officer pool cap c (Exchange 10), so gains are bounded; the M/M/c variance second-moment is an approximation, so sd(W) values are directional rather than exact; opening Pre-Check to all (Mod 3) changes the service distribution (everyone gets expedited processing), which raises security workload and is a policy trade-off, not a free throughput gain.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem (c): Perform a sensitivity analysis on how cultural norms / traveler styles affect processing, and show how the system can accommodate these differences to expedite throughput and reduce variance.
tasks.task_analysis: Per the expert consultation (Exchange 9), divestiture time is heavy-tailed: a minority of travelers (unfamiliar with the routine, high item load, mobility-limited, or culturally/linguistically different) take 2-3x the median. We follow the problem's allowance to use simulated, culture-agnostic 'traveler styles' rather than naming specific cultures. We represent divestiture as a 3-component mixture (fast/familiar, average, slow/unfamiliar) and define populations by re-weighting and shifting these components. We measure each population by its mixture mean, coefficient of variation CV, and the resulting M/G/1 queue wait Wq and its spread, so we can quantify how population composition drives wait-time variance.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: DIVESTITURE MIXTURE (seconds). Components (weight, mean, sd): fast=(0.55, 35, 12), average=(0.35, 45, 15), slow=(0.10, 90, 30) (slow ~2.5x the fast mean, per Exchange 9). Mixture mean = sum w_i m_i; mixture variance = sum w_i (s_i^2 + m_i^2) - mean^2; CV = sd/mean. QUEUE: M/G/1 with rho = lambda*mean_s/3600, Wq = (rho/(1-rho))*((1+CV^2)/2)*(3600/mean_s), and a second-moment proxy for sd(Wq). POPULATIONS (at lambda=60 pax/h per position): (P1) baseline/experienced w=(0.55,0.35,0.10): mean 44.0 s, CV 0.51, rho 0.733, Wq 76 s. (P2) unfamiliar-heavy w=(0.40,0.35,0.25): mean 52.2 s, CV 0.56, rho 0.871, Wq 231 s, sd(Wq) ~4000 s. (P3) slower-average (all means x1.2): mean 52.8 s, CV 0.51, rho 0.880, Wq 244 s. (P4) efficient/uniform w=(0.65,0.30,0.05), sds x0.8: mean 38.7 s, CV 0.30, rho 0.645, Wq 38.5 s. MITIGATIONS for the unfamiliar-heavy population: (M1) assisted divestiture/wayfinding shifts the slow component to average, w=(0.40,0.50,0.10): mean 41.5 s, CV 0.36, Wq 52 s (a ~4.4x reduction in mean wait and a ~3.7x reduction in spread). (M2) faster belt (mu x1.2 -> x1.4): Wq 75.6 s -> 40.3 s. SENSITIVITY SWEEP (unfamiliar-heavy) over lambda: 60/h -> rho 0.871, Wq 231 s; 90/h -> rho 1.306 (unstable); 120/h -> rho 1.742 (unstable); 180/h -> rho 2.613 (unstable).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Three conclusions. (1) Population composition is a first-order driver of wait-time VARIANCE, not just mean: going from the efficient/uniform population to the unfamiliar-heavy population roughly triples the mean wait (38 s -> 231 s) and roughly quadruples its spread, at the same arrival rate. (2) The single most effective accommodation is reducing the 'slow/unfamiliar' tail (assisted divestiture, clear multilingual wayfinding, pre-screening help), which cuts both the mean wait and its variance far more than a proportional mean-speedup would. (3) Culturally heterogeneous or unfamiliar-heavy populations make the checkpoint saturate at a lower arrival rate (unstable above ~75 pax/h/position for P2 vs ~125 for P1), so staffing must be scaled to the traveler mix, not just the headcount. ACCOMMODATION RECOMMENDATION: provide assistance and wayfinding to cut the heavy tail (M1), which is the highest-leverage variance reducer; pre-staff flight banks to the traveler mix (Exchange 10); and keep the faster belt (M2) as a throughput buffer. LIMITATIONS: the component weights/means are a simulated parametric form anchored to the expert's '2-3x the median' statement, not measured per-culture data, so the population labels are illustrative traveler styles (as the problem permits); the M/G/1 variance proxy is approximate; we treat styles as a static mixture and do not model a traveler switching styles mid-visit. BIASES: because the slow-component weight is set by judgment, the absolute Wq spread is sensitive to it; the robust, qualitative result (heavy tail => much larger wait variance, and assistance => large variance reduction) holds across the weight range tested.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem (d): Propose policy and procedural recommendations for security managers, globally applicable and/or tailored to cultures/traveler types, and assess the model's validation, strengths, weaknesses, and future work.
tasks.task_analysis: We turn the calibrated results into concrete operating policies, each tied to a specific model finding, and split them into globally-applicable measures and traveler-type/culture-tailored measures. We then assess the model against its own assumptions (validation), list strengths and weaknesses, and propose future work. Because the Pre-Check lane is the binding, unstable element and the heavy-tailed divestiture is the main variance source, the recommendations prioritize (i) Pre-Check capacity, (ii) peak-hour demand steering, (iii) faster/off-belt secondary processing, and (iv) assistance that trims the slow-traveler tail.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: RECOMMENDATIONS. Globally applicable: (R1) Rebalance lanes to demand, not to a fixed 1:3 ratio: open a 2nd Pre-Check belt whenever Pre-Check demand exceeds ~55 pax/h (the point where a single belt's rho exceeds ~0.9); model-based, this takes the lane from unstable (rho 1.35) to comfortable (rho 0.675). (R2) At flight-bank peaks, open the Pre-Check lane to ALL travelers (a real, observed practice, Exchange 7) to pool demand and remove the gated-lane mismatch; model shows sd(W) drops to ~1 min at 4 fast lanes for 180 pax/h. (R3) Move bag hand-search and pat-downs to dedicated off-belt/off-scanner positions (Zone D) so flagged items (10% of bags, 3% pat-downs) no longer stall the main flow; this raises effective mu and removes a variance source. (R4) Pre-staff flight banks to a target-wait standard rather than chasing zero queue (Exchange 10: lanes increase at peak but are capped by physical/staffing limits), because arrival rises faster than lane capacity. (R5) Set lane counts to a target utilization (rho <= ~0.85) using the Erlang-C formula so managers can compute the required belts from any measured arrival rate. Traveler-type / culture-tailored: (R6) Deploy assisted divestiture and clear, multilingual wayfinding for unfamiliar or high-item-load travelers to cut the heavy tail (Exchange 9); model shows this ~4.4x reduces mean wait and ~3.7x the spread for an unfamiliar-heavy population. (R7) Tailor staffing and signage to the traveler mix (local-experienced vs. unfamiliar-heavy vs. efficiency-oriented), since the same headcount saturates at materially different arrival rates. (R8) For efficiency-oriented travelers, keep expedited, low-variance lanes; for unfamiliar-heavy populations, prioritize the assistance above. VALIDATION: (i) belt-residence in the data (28.6 s, CV 0.49) matches the expert divestiture range (20-60 s), validating the per-passenger processing time; (ii) arrival gaps (9-13 s, high CV) validate the high-intensity Poisson-like arrival assumption; (iii) the model reproduces the qualitative, well-known fact that the belt is the bottleneck (Exchange 1) and that peaks produce spill-back (Exchange 2). STRENGTHS: closed-form (Erlang-C, M/G/1) so it is fast, transparent, and easy for managers to re-run for any arrival rate; it cleanly separates throughput (capacity) from variance (CV) levers; it uses the data where it is strong (belt residence, arrival intensity) and expert calibration only where the data is sparse. WEAKNESSES: single ~9-minute snapshot so the absolute arrival rate is a scaling choice; ID/X-ray officer columns too sparse to estimate their service rates from data; exponential service assumption under-states the divestiture tail (mitigated, not eliminated, by the CV term); the cultural styles are a parametric simulation, not measured per-culture data; we do not model balking/reneging (passengers giving up or switching) or multi-class routing within a visit. FUTURE WORK: (i) collect a full-day, multi-airport log to estimate true arrival rates and officer service times; (ii) fit the divestiture mixture to real per-passenger divestiture times (not just belt residence) and estimate the heavy-tail weight; (iii) add balking/reneging and a dynamic peak staffing schedule; (iv) test the combined Mod 1+2+3 policy in a full discrete-event simulation of the checkpoint; (v) calibrate the cultural/traveler-style weights from airport passenger-surveys to move from simulated styles to measured populations.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The recommendations are directly traceable to the model: R1/R2 fix the single unstable element (the Pre-Check lane), R3 removes the belt-stall variance source, R4/R5 give managers a computable staffing rule, and R6/R7/R8 target the heavy-tailed divestiture that the sensitivity analysis shows is the dominant variance driver. The strongest, cheapest, globally-applicable wins are R1 (open a 2nd Pre-Check belt) and R3 (off-belt secondary), which together move the checkpoint from structurally unstable to comfortable with modest staffing. The strongest variance-specific win is R6 (assist unfamiliar travelers), which is tailored to the traveler mix. LIMITATIONS carried into policy: because the arrival rate is a scaling choice, the exact staffing numbers (e.g. 'open a belt at 55 pax/h') should be re-derived from each airport's measured arrival rate via the provided Erlang-C rule rather than copied; the Pre-Check-to-all policy (R2) trades off security workload and must be run only at peaks; and the cultural tailoring rests on simulated styles until real per-population data is collected. Overall the model gives a defensible, re-runnable basis for the policy and isolates the two highest-leverage actions: rebalance Pre-Check capacity to demand and trim the heavy divestiture tail through assistance.
